story_text.value:
A friend and I built this for our own calls and are sharing it as is. The itch: we kept copy-pasting Granola transcripts into Claude mid-call, and wondered what would happen if the agent just joined.

Two-minute demo: https://youtu.be/XhCSRiiL67A

How it works: a local Electron app joins the Meet in its own browser as a participant. Your agent drives it over MCP (or HTTP): tools to listen, speak, and write to a shared whiteboard. Any MCP agent works; we built for Claude Code first, and Codex and Cursor run it too. It is your actual session, on your machine, in your repo, with your skills, so it can do real work during the call instead of summarizing afterwards.

The hack: by default it does no speech recognition of its own. It reads Meet's live captions, and speaks through a virtual microphone. This is cheap and surprisingly good! (There is also an experimental realtime mode in app preferences that puts OpenAI's speech-to-speech model in the voice seat, with your agent feeding it facts.)

Bring an ElevenLabs key for a better voice. Works with Google Meet and Slack huddles today; Zoom is in progress. Known issues are in the README.

Try it in your next Google Meet and surprise a friend. Let us know what you think!

My frustration with the Apple Music macOS app has been growing over the years.

While I consider the iOS app to be pretty well done (when it comes to UI and performance), the macOS app is a slow disaster. story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Nick. I'm a self-taught programmer with some B.S. in Applied Math, currently working construction but for the past few years have been building something that I think is extremely cool which is AA! My goal was to create a tool to hopefully help folks get jobs, and in the process perhaps gather and showcase job market data from a different perspective that I believe contains stories, ideas, and considerations worthy of sharing.

As of right now, AA has never successfully submitted anything, but I'm hoping that will all change very soon. Worst-case scenario users were my target audience with the goal being have it run efficiently, accurately, and reliably! I figured, if I could achieve something capable of functioning in this way then that would mean maximum availability to those who need it most.

- Customization Central Tons of ways to run: clone it, from a Flashdrive, inside Docker? Perhaps you only want it to collect qualified/aligned links or have it just apply to the links you provide or even Human in the Loop with set checkpoints? Avoid LinkedIn and Indeed and other login required sites, no problem!

- Download AA to a flash drive and plug it into a local library computer. I got the opportunity to work with my local library to offer folks sessions where they get AA up and running and while it does its thing they go and learn useful job skills and practice.

- Autonomy through Geometry: no hardcoded selectors anywhere. AA reads pages geometrically instead: Kuhn–Munkres assignment to optimally pair form labels to their inputs, convex hulls and VIPS-style segmentation for regions. Pure Python, deterministic, zero I/O, sitting behind ports.

As I mentioned, I made this to be a tool to help people find and get employed in this tough job market. Unfortunately, I knew this could only do so much which is why I tried to expand on that very idea!

- AA as a research instrument. Off by default; users can opt in, or withdraw, which deletes everything including the signing key. Zero PII collected, your profile can be encrypted with AES-256, the research data can be exported anytime, every row gets signed, and you can re-run any analysis and get byte-identical output.

- Biggest flaw to consider: once AA starts running, that device is dedicated to it until completion is reached or you end it early.

If this project caught your interest or attention there's a lot more to explore in my repo and would love for folks to go try and clone it and look around as I just pushed updates to hopefully make --install and --uninstall simple and non-destructive also use caution running session's as I was trying to impress a girl on Sunday and thought I'd try and show her my sick coding abilities and well within 6 seconds I managed to break absolutely everything which resulted in me saying saying wait every 2 minutes for 30 minutes until she left. Any who, if you are known as or even consider yourself one of the individuals below...

- Economist: What high-level things can I calculate for to have my data be more significant or applicable? What unique data could I gather that I may not consider insightful but is?

- Research Software Engineer: How bad is the damage? Any knowledge you can give me I would greatly appreciate!

- Mathematician: Sup nerd? Please look at my Math subsystem, Form Engine, Clingo code and tell me what to fix?

- Statistician: Checking out my signals_taxonomy.md would be dope and tell me the type of data I could perhaps report on that could be useful, beneficial, or applicable to current research?

- Lawyer: Would this perhaps get me in some bit of trouble?

- Any other kind of PhD person: Y'all are smart; if you're interested, ask me about my project in a way that relates to your field?

I'd love any feedback, input, suggestions, questionable insights, and funny insults that you'd like to toss my way!

story_text.value:
We pulled out the semantic layer from our other app (Strata.do) and made it a standalone service. Now anyone can build data apps with an integrated deterministic, secure, and fast query layer.

How it works: 1. Use the zsql cli to build your model locally 2. zsql deploy (self hosted versions soon) 3. Post a query spec to your projects end point 4. Get back SQL

We never connect to your data warehouse or see any actual data. We only see your model and generate valid sql's.

This is an alternative to using Cube, MetricFlow, Semantic Views, and various other solutions. See our comparison table for the key differences: https://www.0sql.io/#compare

Thanks for checking it out! What do you think??

story_text.value:
I'm obsessed with Egyptology. During covid, I wanted to get a hieratic tattoo. For those who don't know, hieratic is the cursive form of hieroglyphs that was used in day-to-day life in ancient Egypt. It's as old as hieroglyphs.

I then went on a mission to have a sentence translated into hieratic. Luckily, in 2022, I was able to commission an Oxford Egyptologist to write it for me. After that, I took it to a hieratic specialist I found on Instagram to redraw it with "biblical" accuracy.

When generative AI came out, I realized that models very rarely identify hieratic and almost never translate it correctly. Every single time a new model came out, I ended up testing my sentence and hieratic texts in general, and I realized this could actually become a benchmark. Since so many benchmarks are becoming saturated, we need to find weird ways to test new models.

That's why I decided to build HieraticBench.

The first version of the benchmark has 268 items, including real documents, signs, and other Egyptian scripts, which I used as controls, as well as my unpublished sentence in two different renditions. The current state-of-the-art foundation models are hilariously bad at identifying my sentence, especially the one the Egyptologist wrote with her pen. Some of them said Tibetan, Urdu, Korean, and, funnily enough, "Reformed Egyptian," which is from the Book of Mormon.

On real documents, the best model in the benchmark identified hieratic correctly 95% of the time, and the best score for reading individual signs was around 13%. That's when we tell the model specifically that it's hieratic. None of them can really translate a sealed sentence that's never been published and has no answer key.

I haven't run every model on every task just to keep costs down. My next steps were to run Astra and Gemini 3.1 Pro on real documents. Currently, only the Claude models have done the sign readings.

And just FYI, I have no experience whatsoever running benchmarks or evaluations, so not 100% sure I scored things right.

Things we need: - Running the models I haven't covered - More sealed sentences and labeled signs

If you know hieratic or have an Egyptologist friend, reach out at hieraticbench@veeza.ai.

Source code: https://github.com/alymoursy/hieraticbench

I'll be around to answer questions.

title.value: Show HN: HieraticBench – Can AI read ancient Egyptian handwriting?

story_text.value:
One of the annoying things about YouTube is that it is really good at catching my attention, but I have little control over what kind of feed it can show me, so it becomes distracting instead. I don't want to hide recommendations entirely though, I just don't want all my interests mixed into one feed.

So I wondered if I could have separate YouTube profiles for different interests, but make creating one as simple as picking a few topics instead of having to create or connect another Google account.

So I built Gretel, a desktop app. It uses YT.js to access YouTube, and it runs locally so the requests come from my own machine rather than a server.

I create profiles, each with their own topics. Gretel then searches YouTube for the topics, collects candidate videos, and creates an embedding that is used to filter videos later on.

From the candidate videos, Gretel fetches related videos and continuously expands outward while filtering unrelated videos. This creates the base feed. After that, as I watch videos, the topic embeddings are continuously updated, and at the same time Gretel persists the YouTube sessions so the recommendations adapt as well.

I have been working on Gretel on and off for a while. It's beta: usable but still rough. I am curious if, after using a profile for a while, the feed actually starts converging toward what you wanted. Bug reports and contributions are welcome too.

You can sign in with Google to use the included embedding credits, or bring your own OpenRouter key. Other providers and local embedding models are coming.

This is actually a reincarnation of a project I did almost 10 years ago (GitSpo). I index social sites (X, Bluesky, Reddit, HackerNews, etc) and track content that mentions any GitHub repository. If you are an open-source author – this gives you a daily or weekly summary of all social mentions of your project. If you are evaluating open-source projects, this allows you to validate them by observing that has been said about these projects in public forums.

Provided as a public service. Doesn't cost you anything.
